questions.prompt: What does a discriminative model like a spam classifier actually learn?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: A boundary that separates categories — essentially p(label | input) — rather than the structure of the inputs themselves

A discriminative model, like the classifiers from the ML course, learns to map an input to a label by finding the boundary between classes — it models p(label | input), not the data's own structure.
keyPoints: A discriminative model, like the classifiers from the ML course, learns to map an input to a label by finding the boundary between classes — it models p(label | input), not the data's own structure.

questions.prompt: Why is evaluating a generative model harder than evaluating a classifier?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: For open-ended generation tasks, there's no single correct output to compare against, unlike a classifier's known correct label

A classifier has one correct label to check against (as in the ML course's metrics). An open-ended generation task like writing a poem has many equally valid possible outputs, so there's no single ground truth to compare against directly.
keyPoints: A classifier has one correct label to check against (as in the ML course's metrics).
An open-ended generation task like writing a poem has many equally valid possible outputs, so there's no single ground truth to compare against directly.

questions.prompt: What is the key limitation of greedy decoding?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: It makes a purely local decision at each step with no look-ahead, so the token that looks best right now can lead to a worse overall sequence than a different early choice would have

Greedy decoding commits to the single best-looking next token at each step without considering how that choice affects the rest of the sequence, which can lead it into a worse overall outcome than a less locally-optimal first choice.
keyPoints: Greedy decoding commits to the single best-looking next token at each step without considering how that choice affects the rest of the sequence, which can lead it into a worse overall outcome than a less locally-optimal first choice.

questions.prompt: Why is running diffusion directly on full-resolution pixel data computationally expensive?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Each of the many iterative denoising steps has to operate on the full, large pixel tensor, and doing this repeatedly across dozens to hundreds of steps adds up to a large computational cost

Since diffusion requires many iterative refinement steps, and each step processes the full data tensor, operating directly on large raw pixel data multiplies that per-step cost by the number of iterations — a substantial computational burden.
keyPoints: Since diffusion requires many iterative refinement steps, and each step processes the full data tensor, operating directly on large raw pixel data multiplies that per-step cost by the number of iterations — a substantial computational burden.

questions.prompt: Why is directly modeling the probability of an entire sentence described as intractable in this lesson?
questions.referenceAnswer: The lesson states that modeling an entire sentence's probability directly is intractable simply due to the enormous number of possible sentences, motivating the token-by-token factorization instead.
keyPoints: The lesson states that modeling an entire sentence's probability directly is intractable simply due to the enormous number of possible sentences, motivating the token-by-token factorization instead.

choices.text: Because there are far too many possible sentences to model directly
Because sentences don't have any probability associated with them
Because only single words have probabilities, not sequences
Because tractability only matters for images, not text

questions.prompt: What does top-k sampling do at each generation step?
questions.referenceAnswer: Top-k limits the candidate pool to a fixed number (k) of the most likely tokens at each step, preventing the model from ever sampling from the long tail of very unlikely tokens.
keyPoints: Top-k limits the candidate pool to a fixed number (k) of the most likely tokens at each step, preventing the model from ever sampling from the long tail of very unlikely tokens.

choices.text: It keeps every possible token as a candidate, with no restriction
It restricts sampling to only the k highest-probability tokens, discarding the rest of the vocabulary for that step
It always selects the single most likely token, with no randomness
It only applies to image generation, not text

questions.prompt: What does constrained decoding do at each decoding step that plain prompting does not, per this lesson?
questions.referenceAnswer: Constrained decoding modifies the decoding process itself so invalid tokens are never even considered as candidates, unlike prompting, which only nudges probabilities without enforcing hard constraints.
keyPoints: Constrained decoding modifies the decoding process itself so invalid tokens are never even considered as candidates, unlike prompting, which only nudges probabilities without enforcing hard constraints.

choices.text: It restricts the candidate tokens to only those consistent with a target grammar or schema
It removes the need for any decoding step entirely
It forces the model to always output the exact same fixed template
It only works for generating unconstrained natural language

questions.prompt: What does classifier-free guidance compare at each denoising step?
questions.referenceAnswer: Classifier-free guidance works by comparing what the model predicts with the prompt versus without it, then amplifying the difference — pushing the final result further in the direction the prompt suggests.
keyPoints: Classifier-free guidance works by comparing what the model predicts with the prompt versus without it, then amplifying the difference — pushing the final result further in the direction the prompt suggests.

choices.text: Two completely unrelated models with no shared training
The conditional (prompt-guided) prediction and the unconditional (no-prompt) prediction, pushing the result further toward the prompt-conditioned direction
The training loss from two different epochs
The output resolution before and after compression

questions.prompt: How is the text embedding delivered into the diffusion model's denoising steps, per this lesson?
questions.referenceAnswer: The lesson explains that the text embedding is fed into the denoising network at each step, often through cross-attention — the same mechanism connecting encoder and decoder in the transformers course.
keyPoints: The lesson explains that the text embedding is fed into the denoising network at each step, often through cross-attention — the same mechanism connecting encoder and decoder in the transformers course.

choices.text: Often via cross-attention, feeding into the denoising network at each step
By replacing the noise schedule entirely
By converting it back into raw text before generation begins
It is not used during denoising at all, only afterward

questions.prompt: Why is combining information from text, images, and audio into one model a genuinely hard architectural problem?
questions.referenceAnswer: Text, images, and audio have very different native structures and scales, so deciding how and where to fuse information from each into a shared representation is a nontrivial architectural challenge, not a simple bolt-on.
keyPoints: Text, images, and audio have very different native structures and scales, so deciding how and where to fuse information from each into a shared representation is a nontrivial architectural challenge, not a simple bolt-on.

choices.text: It's actually trivial and requires no special design consideration

These modalities have fundamentally different structure and scale (discrete sequential tokens vs. dense spatial grids vs. high-rate continuous waveforms), making it a real design challenge to combine them meaningfully
All modalities are represented identically once tokenized, so there's nothing to solve
Multimodal models never actually combine different modalities in practice

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a model to 'amplify' bias, as opposed to simply reflecting it, per this lesson?
questions.referenceAnswer: The lesson describes amplification as models showing associations skewed beyond what the raw training data proportions alone would suggest, not just a simple reflection of those proportions.
keyPoints: The lesson describes amplification as models showing associations skewed beyond what the raw training data proportions alone would suggest, not just a simple reflection of those proportions.

choices.text: In documented cases, models have shown associations stronger than what raw training data statistics alone would predict
Amplification means the model perfectly mirrors training data proportions with zero distortion
Amplification refers exclusively to increasing an audio model's output volume
Amplification means a model completely removes all bias from its output
